conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having nausea and vomiting since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since about 8 AM. I was vomiting every 15 minutes and couldn’t keep anything down. The pain is back too—burning, right here in the upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you had laparoscopic surgery five days ago for a possible hernia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they thought it was a paraduodenal hernia, but said they didn’t find one. They fixed a defect in the colon instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. The CT scan from the ER shows no signs of a surgical complication—no free air, no abscess. The surgeons reviewed it and think this is likely a flare-up of your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not from the surgery? I was worried something went wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the imaging doesn’t show any issues from the surgery. Your symptoms match what you’ve had before—chronic nausea and delayed stomach emptying. We’re going to admit you for a few days to help control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had this for years. But it’s been worse lately, and I’ve lost weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common with gastroparesis. We’ve placed a nasogastric tube to rest your stomach and will give you IV fluids and anti-nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube is uncomfortable, but I’ll do what I need to. What medicine are you giving me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started IV Zofran, 8 mg. It’s helped many patients like you. We’ll keep monitoring and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since the tube was placed, and the nausea is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The chest X-ray confirmed the NG tube is in the right place. We also checked your labs—your potassium is a bit low, so we’re adding some to your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’ve been feeling weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Low potassium can cause fatigue and muscle weakness. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows no obstruction. Air is moving through your bowels, and the NG tube is still in place. This supports that it’s gastroparesis, not a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Can I try drinking something soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to keep your stomach at rest for now. But you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea has been gone for over 24 hours. We’re going to stop the NG tube and start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips at first. We’ll see how you tolerate it. If you do well, we’ll advance to a soft diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about my regular meds? I take omeprazole, Celexa, and Synthroid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been giving you those by mouth since yesterday. Your thyroid and acid reflux are stable, so we’re continuing them as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastroenterologist came by this morning. He agrees this is a gastroparesis flare. He recommends continuing your dromperidone and eating six small, low-fat meals a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing that, but it’s hard to stick to. Are there any other treatments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: He mentioned a repeat gastric emptying study could help guide future treatment, but for now, diet and medication are the mainstays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. My blood pressure has been high lately too—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your diastolic pressure was elevated, but we didn’t start new meds. Your primary doctor should check it after you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well on the soft diet. No nausea or vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What should I do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your regular medications. Stick to small, frequent, low-fat meals. Advance your diet slowly as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your gastroenterologist or primary doctor. If it’s severe, go to the ER. But you’re in much better shape now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning are stable. We’ve updated your discharge meds—omeprazole is now 20 mg instead of 40, but everything else is the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that okay? I’ve been on 40 mg for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your reflux is well-controlled, and 20 mg is sufficient. It’s a common adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And I should follow up with my PCP and gastroenterologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll help manage your gastroparesis long-term. We’ll send them a summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you home today. Take it easy, eat small meals, and keep up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this wasn’t something serious from the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT and exam confirmed no surgical complications. This was a recurrence of your chronic condition, well-managed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ll be more careful with my diet going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. And reach out if symptoms return—we’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we hope not to see you back soon!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here. Have a good day!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with nausea and vomiting again—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up this morning feeling nauseous and vomited just spit—no food, nothing. I haven’t eaten anything today. It’s been like this for a few days now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain in your belly when you vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a general ache, nothing sharp. No diarrhea or blood in stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you mentioned back pain too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s usually there, but today it’s worse—especially when I move. It’s a nagging pain, maybe a 6 out of 10.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No numbness, tingling, or trouble with bladder or bowels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get some labs and imaging. Your white blood cell count is high—17.4—so we’re checking for infection, but your chest X-ray looks clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. We’ll keep an eye on it. We also did a spine X-ray because of your back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had back issues before, but it’s never this bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the T-spine film back. There’s a new compression fracture in two of your mid-back bones. That’s likely why the pain is worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fracture? But I didn’t fall or anything!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With chronic conditions like yours and possible osteoporosis, bones can weaken. Sometimes even normal movement can cause a fracture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not an emergency, but it needs attention. We’ll manage the pain and make sure you follow up with your primary doctor about bone health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back—no infection. The high white count is likely from stress or inflammation, not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not needed. We’re focusing on your gastroparesis and nutrition. You’ve lost 50 pounds in a year—that’s a big concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just can’t keep food down. I’ve tried everything—meds, Botox, small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re talking with your gastroenterologist. They want a J-tube, but surgery wants to try a temporary feeding tube first—goes past the stomach into the small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A tube in my nose again? I hate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s temporary. Helps us see if feeding past the stomach works before doing surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Dobhoff tube is in—placed past your stomach. We’ll start slow feeding today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? How will I feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people don’t feel it much. We’ll watch for nausea. If you tolerate it, this could be a step toward better nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’ve had the feeding tube for two days, no nausea or vomiting. Your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I didn’t even notice it after the first day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. It means your body can handle nutrition past the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I pulled the tube out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did? Are you feeling okay? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. I just want to go home. I’m tired of being here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we need to plan next steps. The tube worked well—your team may still recommend a permanent J-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Can I go home now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on discharge. But please follow up with your GI and surgeon to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low when you came in—2.6. That can make you weak and affect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 4.1 now. We’ll send you home with potassium pills—one daily, especially if you vomit again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—up to 170/99. We started you on metoprolol. Stress and pain can raise it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely, but long-term it’s important to control. Keep taking the medication and monitor at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your PCP can reassess once things settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your nausea is controlled, labs are stable, and you’re walking fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been using ketorolac and Valium as needed. You’ll go home with naproxen—a similar medicine—for one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fracture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your primary doctor about osteoporosis. They may start treatment to strengthen your bones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same ones: citalopram, levothyroxine, omeprazole. New ones: Zofran and Compazine for nausea if it returns, potassium daily, and naproxen for back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the feeding tube decision?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still important to discuss with GI and surgery. The temporary tube worked, so a permanent one might help long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, get your labs done next week—Chem 10—and fax the results to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if nausea returns or pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hopefully not! But we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with the spine fracture. No heavy lifting for several weeks. Use caution with movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the lidocaine patch for back pain if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the discharge papers are ready. You’re free to go when you’re set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, one last question—can I drive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you’re not on strong pain meds and feel alert, yes. But listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m off the IV meds, so I think I’m okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then yes, you can drive. Just take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. We’ll make sure to support your nutrition. You were given some medications in the ER—Zofran for nausea, Reglan, and pain meds. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain and nausea are much better now. I don’t feel any abdominal pain right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your heart rate was high when you arrived—110. That’s likely from dehydration and discomfort. We’ve started IV fluids and potassium to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having low potassium before too. It’s always a problem when I can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw your potassium was low again. We’re replacing it carefully through the IV. We also checked your blood gases and found a mild acidosis, which we’re monitoring as your fluids improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Acidosis? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon when someone hasn’t been eating or drinking well. As your body gets rehydrated and starts getting nutrition, it should resolve. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just feel like I’m not bouncing back like I used to after these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that. You’ve been through a lot. This is your fourth admission in recent months, right? What are your goals for this hospitalization?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, I think it’s time. I want to go ahead with the J tube. I’ve been scared of it, but I talked to a friend who has a feeding tube, and it helped me see it could really help me get stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big step, and I’m glad you’re feeling ready. Your GI doctor has recommended it, and the surgery team agrees it may be the best long-term option for your nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I can’t keep living like this—admitting every few weeks, losing weight, feeling awful. I want to feel better and get my strength back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my nausea?

conversation_lines.text: Not directly. It was just a precaution. Your symptoms are still most consistent with your gastroparesis flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have that back pain from before. Is that being looked at?

conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know from your last admission that you have a pathologic fracture in your spine from osteoporosis. That’s likely the source of your back pain. We’re managing it with medication and will continue to address your bone health as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on thyroid meds and for depression too. Are we adjusting anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued your usual doses of levothyroxine and your antidepressant. No changes needed there. We’re also watching your IBS, but it doesn’t seem to be active now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—surgery has reviewed your case. They agree a J tube would be appropriate. They want to see you improve a bit more first, but they’re planning to schedule the procedure as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so not here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They prefer to do it electively. You’re doing better, but they want you fully optimized—nutritionally and medically—before the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just don’t want to keep delaying it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I promise we’ll make it a priority. In the meantime, we’re arranging a home health referral so you can get support with nutrition and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Your nausea is controlled, you’re not vomiting, and your labs are much better. We’re going to start transitioning you to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I be on any new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your anti-nausea meds for now—Reglan and Zofran as needed. You’ll also keep potassium supplements until your levels stay stable with better intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the J tube plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery will call you to schedule the procedure. Your GI doctor will coordinate the feeding plan. We’ll also send referrals for bone health and nutrition counseling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel hopeful this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ve reviewed your discharge instructions, and your prescriptions are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ll follow up with everyone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if nausea returns or you can’t keep fluids down. Otherwise, focus on rest and preparing for your J tube. This is a positive step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening and helping me make this decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my acidosis? I remember last time I had that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, mild anion gap acidosis with low bicarbonate and ketones in your urine. It’s likely from not eating—starvation ketosis. We’re correcting it with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t eaten much the past few days. I just don’t feel like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with gastroparesis flares. We’ll keep you on bowel rest today and monitor your labs tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs look much better. Bicarbonate is now 23, so the acidosis has resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m still spitting up saliva, but no vomiting since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’re going to start your tube feeds again at a low rate, as recommended by nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that Isosource again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, full strength at 15 mL per hour, increasing slowly. We’ll watch for any nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The enteral feeding started at 12, and you’re tolerating it well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t feel any worse. That’s a win.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to keep you another day to make sure the feeds stay stable and you remain symptom-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’d rather be safe. Any other test results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed a small 12 mm nodule on your left adrenal gland. It’s unchanged from before, but you should follow up with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not urgent. It’s been stable, so it’s likely benign, but your doctor should check it periodically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make an appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are all stable. Potassium 3.9, bicarbonate 23. You’ve had no nausea, and the feeds are at 25 mL/hr.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you keep doing well. We’ll discharge you later this morning. We’ll send you home with your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I restart my citalopram? I missed it yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting it today. Also, your levothyroxine and PPI are continuing as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube feeds? Should I increase the rate at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, increase by 10 mL every 6 hours as tolerated, up to 45 mL/hr. Call GI if you have nausea or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Keep following up with your GI doctor and PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll take it slow and watch my symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call us if vomiting returns or you can’t keep feeds down. Otherwise, see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been nauseous for two days. After just a few sips of a fizzy lime drink—something I’ve had before—I suddenly felt sick and vomited. Since then, I’ve been dry heaving every 15 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any blood in the vomit? Or abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood in the vomit, but when I made myself vomit a few times, I noticed a little blood on my fingers. I don’t have belly pain, but my stomach muscles are sore from all the heaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And any fever, chills, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a low-grade fever, I think. And I’ve had more bowel movements—about five yesterday, some loose, some normal. No blood in the stool, but I felt urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. You have a history of gastroparesis and a GJ tube. When was your last tube feeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two nights ago. I skipped it last night because I was too nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll start you on IV fluids and anti-nausea meds. We also checked some labs. Your blood work shows a metabolic acidosis, likely from not eating—your body is burning fat for energy, which produces ketones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why I feel so weak? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it gets worse, but we’re treating it with fluids and will restart your tube feeds soon. It should resolve quickly now that we’re supporting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. My blood pressure was high in the ER—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your BP was elevated, but it’s likely due to dehydration and stress. It’s already coming down. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no need for new meds right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my potassium was low last time—did you check that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 3.3, which is a bit low, likely from vomiting. We’ve added potassium to your IV fluids to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been doing this self-vomiting thing because it helps the nausea, but I know it’s not good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand it gives temporary relief, but it can irritate your esophagus. Your recent EGD showed esophagitis and a small ulcer, so we want to avoid further trauma. That’s probably where the blood on your fingers came from.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. So I should stop doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll manage your nausea with IV medications instead—metoclopramide, ondansetron, and a little lorazepam if needed. You’re NPO for now, meaning no food or drink by mouth, to let your stomach rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. What about my tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart them soon, once your nausea is under better control. Nutrition team will guide the timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea has improved, and labs are trending better. Your acidosis is resolving—your bicarbonate is up to 18 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can start eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet by mouth, but we’re starting enteral nutrition through your GJ tube today. It’s a concentrated formula to give you calories and help correct the starvation state.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And my stool test came back negative for C. diff, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, good catch. Your stool tested negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and parasites. No infection found, which supports this being a gastroparesis flare, not infectious colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not an infection. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Blood cultures were also negative, so no sign of systemic infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve done well overnight. You tolerated the tube feeds, and your nausea is much better. We’re going to try a clear liquid diet by mouth today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips of water, broth, or apple juice. We’ll go slow—if you keep it down, we’ll advance it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my labs? Is the acidosis gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your bicarbonate is now 23, and anion gap is normal. The starvation ketosis has resolved with nutrition and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such good news. What about my potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium dipped to 3.0 this morning, so we gave a supplement. It’s now 4.5 and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’ve kept down clear liquids, your vitals are stable, and labs are normal. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Are my medications the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home on your usual meds: lansoprazole, levothyroxine, citalopram, and your anti-nausea meds—metoclopramide four times a day now, and ondansetron or lorazepam as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take the metoclopramide regularly. Any diet advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue with clear liquids today, then advance slowly to soft foods. Avoid fizzy drinks and dairy for now—they can trigger symptoms. Restart full tube feeds tonight if tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your PCP in a few days. They’ll monitor your progress and review any pending stool tests, though they’re likely negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep using your tube for nutrition, take your meds, and call if nausea returns or you can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee. I saw you came in last night with abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had this kind of pain before — it’s in my upper belly, right in the middle. It started a day ago and felt sharp and crampy. I think it’s related to that barium test I had earlier this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, I see here you had an upper GI series as part of your gastroparesis evaluation. That involved drinking barium, which can sometimes slow things down even more in people with delayed stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. After that test, I started feeling worse — really nauseous, couldn’t keep anything down. It felt just like my past flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We did a KUB — that’s an abdominal X-ray — to check if there was any blockage. Good news: no obstruction. But we did see barium still moving through your colon, which confirms it’s passed out of the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not stuck? That’s a relief. I was worried something was blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing’s blocked. The issue seems to be a flare of your gastroparesis, likely triggered by the large volume of barium. Your stomach just couldn’t handle it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What will we do now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO — nothing by mouth — for now to give your stomach a rest. You’re getting IV fluids to stay hydrated, and we’ve started IV medications like Reglan and lorazepam to help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken Reglan at home. Is that better than Zofran?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially for gastroparesis. Zofran helps with nausea but doesn’t move the stomach. Reglan actually helps your stomach empty faster, so we prefer it for your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ll stick with Reglan then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also giving you IV pantoprazole for your GERD, since you can’t take pills right now. And your levothyroxine is being given IV to keep your thyroid levels stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about my other meds — like citalopram and vitamin D?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held those for now since you’re NPO. Once you’re eating again, we’ll restart them. No need to worry — a short break is safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. How long will I need to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess tomorrow. If your nausea improves and you can tolerate liquids, we’ll start you on a clear diet and likely discharge you in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning! I’m glad to see you looking more comfortable. Your nurse said you haven’t vomited since yesterday and your pain is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel a lot better. The nausea is mostly gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to try starting you on a clear liquid diet — things like broth, apple juice, and tea. We’ll go slowly to make sure your stomach can handle it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water first?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve already been sipping water, and that’s fine. The clear liquids are the next step. We’ll monitor you closely after each intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the blood test from yesterday? Anything concerning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly normal. Your potassium was a bit low at 3.4, so we’re giving a little in your IV. And your alkaline phosphatase was slightly elevated — we’ll repeat that as an outpatient to make sure it’s not a concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it can also be from bone. Since it’s only mildly high and your other liver tests are normal, we’re not worried now. Just a follow-up to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to get that checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Now that you’re improving, we’ll keep you on liquids today and aim to send you home tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be wonderful. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning! You made it through the night without any nausea and tolerated full liquids well. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel really good. No pain, no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re going to discharge you today. You can go home and gradually advance your diet — start with soft foods, then see how you do with regular meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I avoid another barium test in the future?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that with your specialist. For now, just know that this reaction was likely due to the volume. If you need imaging again, we can explore alternatives or take precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart all your home medications — lansoprazole, Reglan, levothyroxine, citalopram, and the others — exactly as before. Take Reglan 30 minutes before meals to help with stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lorazepam for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use it as needed for anxiety or nausea, but try Reglan first since it’s better for your stomach. And call your doctor if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you so much for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You’re being discharged in stable condition. Follow up with your PCP and your GI doctor soon, especially to review the alkaline phosphatase and discuss the gastric pacer option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment already scheduled. I’ll mention it there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and feel free to call if anything changes before your visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Patel. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis and a J-tube, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be stress? I’ve been anxious lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stress can definitely trigger it. We’ll manage your symptoms and keep an eye on things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show a slightly low bicarbonate—18—which means mild acidosis. But your kidney function is normal, so it’s likely from not eating or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level. It should improve as you start keeping food down. We’re giving you IV fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white blood cell count is up—from 9.1 to 13.4. That’s called leukocytosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I have an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but you’re not running a fever, and your urine and chest X-ray are clear. It could be from the stress of illness or mild gastroenteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we don’t know for sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. But since you’re not septic, we’re not starting antibiotics. We’ll watch it and repeat the test before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Nausea is less, and I sipped some broth without throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll try advancing your diet to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my regular meds? I usually take bethanechol and lansoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted both. Bethanechol helps your stomach empty, and lansoprazole protects against reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also been using the lorazepam for nausea when it gets bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. It helps with both nausea and anxiety. We’ll keep it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight. You kept down toast and applesauce. We’ll try a regular diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. I’m hungry, honestly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just go slow—small, low-fat meals. That’s best for your stomach right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your bicarbonate is now 23—perfect. The acidosis has resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the white blood cells?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still elevated at 13, but you’re clinically improving. It’s likely a stress response. We’ll check it again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about infection later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. But your PCP should check your WBC in a few days to make sure it’s coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full meals and feel steady. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I do at home to avoid another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to small, frequent, low-fat meals. Avoid heavy or greasy foods. Stay on your bethanechol and lansoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the J-tube? Should I restart tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need. You’re using it only for meds, and that’s fine. No sign the tube needs changing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—citalopram, thyroid pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your regular medications. We’ve listed them in your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final blood work shows your WBC is still 13.4, but you’re doing well. We think it’s safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The elevation is likely reactive. But please follow up with your doctor in a few days to repeat the test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re tolerating food, nausea is gone, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: small meals, stay hydrated, and follow up with your PCP to check your white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And call if nausea comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Or if you develop fever, severe pain, or can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll send your discharge instructions to your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.text: Really good. No nausea, and I ate a sandwich earlier.

conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re cleared to go home. Rest well and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you have a ride home and all your prescriptions?

conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your J-tube site looks clean. Keep it dry and monitor for redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: Good. Stay on top of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be feeling normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s hold off on oral intake for now. We’ll focus on the tube feeds and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look much better. Potassium is now 4.0, and bicarbonate is 25 — completely normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. I’m feeling less shaky too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lactate also came down from 2.1 to 0.9, which means your body is no longer under stress from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that was from not keeping fluids down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. When you vomit a lot, your body can’t maintain circulation well, but you’re back on track now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try a little apple juice through the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can add some clear liquids through the tube, yes. Let’s start with half-strength and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight — no nausea, and you kept all the feeds down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually feel hungry for the first time in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. We’ll switch you to your full tube feeding formula today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And can I stop the IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since you’re not having pain or nausea, we’ll discontinue the IV medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling really good. Do you think I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. But we want to make sure you’re stable and have a plan for managing flares at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to keep coming back to the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed this with your GI team. Since you’ve had three hospitalizations this month, we’re going to send you home with morphine and lorazepam tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I can’t swallow them when I’m nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You can crush them and put them through your J-tube. That way, you can treat symptoms early at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That could really help. I wish we’d tried this sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also keep your other meds — levothyroxine, citalopram, omeprazole — going through the tube as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my vitamin D?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that twice a month as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I walked down the hall twice today. I’m feeling stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Your exam shows your abdomen is soft and not tender anymore, and your bowel sounds are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m really ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you continue to do well overnight, we’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel like a new person.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Remember to use the crushed lorazepam and morphine through your tube if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I have my follow-up with Dr. ___ next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and another appointment with your other GI doctor. They’ll help manage your gastroparesis long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to keep those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going home with services to help with your care. Someone will check in with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I live alone, so that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to call your doctor or come back if symptoms worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just waiting for the discharge papers. I’m so ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring them shortly. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve packed everything. Can I ask one more thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I use the meds at home and feel better, should I still call my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. Even if you improve, we want them to know what happened and adjust your plan if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll call right after I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we hope not to see you back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team. I know you’ve been having severe abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about what brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had terrible cramping for two days—no bowel movements, no gas. I couldn’t keep anything down, not even through my tube. It felt worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis and a feeding tube. We did a CT scan, and it showed something serious—your cecum, part of your colon, has twisted. That’s called a cecal volvulus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Twisted? Is that why I couldn’t pass anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The twist is blocking your bowel. Worse, the blood supply is compromised—there’s early signs of ischemia. This needs surgery, and soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? Again? I’ve had so many… What kind of surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do an exploratory laparotomy. We’ll remove the twisted part of your colon—the right side—and reconnect your intestine. There’s also something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT suggests the wires from your old gastric pacemaker may have caused the twist. They’re looping into your bowel. We’ll remove the device and wires during the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I forgot I even had that pacemaker. Is it dangerous to remove?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safe, and necessary. Leaving it could cause more problems. We’ve discussed this with your family, and we have your consent. We’ll prepare you for the OR now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through surgery. You had a right hemicolectomy and the pacemaker with its wires was removed. The anastomosis looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I feel? I’m so groggy… Was everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgery went well—no complications. You’re on a PCA pump for pain. You have an NG tube for now, and we’re giving fluids and antibiotics through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to wait for your bowel to wake up. We’ll start tube feeds once we hear bowel sounds and you pass gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your NG tube is out. You’re passing gas, and your belly is less distended. We’ll keep you NPO for now, but we’re close to starting feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My throat was so sore from the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was high but is coming down. That means the infection risk is improving. We’re still holding off on feeds—just a little longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start your tube feeds today—slowly, at half goal. We’ll monitor for nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m still feeling a bit nauseous. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially after surgery and with your history. We’ll give you anti-nausea meds and go slow. If you tolerate this, we’ll increase tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well with the feeds. We’re increasing to full rate. Your labs are stable, and you’re walking more each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today, we’re exchanging your GJ tube to one with separate G and J ports. It’ll give us more flexibility with feeding and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a big procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s done endoscopically with light sedation. You’ll be back soon, and we’ll restart feeds through the new tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube exchange went smoothly. You’re back on full feeds. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit sore at the site, but okay. Still nauseous when I try to eat by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expected that. We’re going to try clamping your tube for short periods to see if you can tolerate oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve always had trouble keeping food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we need to assess if it’s mechanical or motility-related. We’ll schedule a gastric emptying study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastric emptying study came back normal. Liquids are leaving your stomach at a normal rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why do I feel so full and nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an upper GI study too. It shows your Nissen fundoplication is intact, no narrowing. But there’s moderate esophageal dysmotility—your esophagus isn’t moving food down well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my stomach, it’s my esophagus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That explains the nausea when you try to eat. We’ll adjust your diet and add a new anti-nausea med. You’ll follow up with GI after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating clamping trials better. We’re advancing your diet to regular food in small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a few bites yesterday and didn’t vomit. That’s progress!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your incision is healing well—no redness or drainage. Pain is controlled with oral meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’re walking independently, tolerating a regular diet, and your feeds are at goal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your labs are stable, vitals are good. Home health will help with your GJ tube and feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue levothyroxine, citalopram, omeprazole. We’re adding dronabinol and trimethobenzamide for nausea, as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your surgeon in two weeks. GI will evaluate your esophageal dysmotility. Call us if you have fever, vomiting, or incision problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about lifting or driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lifting over five pounds for four weeks. Don’t drive while on pain meds. Showering is okay—just keep the incision dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the steri-strips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll fall off on their own. Remove any left after ten days. Staples will be removed at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing the tube at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home health will train you and your caregiver. They’ll visit several times a week at first. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep resting, stay hydrated, and keep walking. You’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, you’re tolerating everything well. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t wait to be home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be here if you need us. Take care, and see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I get the flu shot this year?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. It’s especially important with your medical history. Your primary care can give it in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ll schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Rest well, and don’t hesitate to call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned that the hard way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re doing great. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Call us if anything’s unclear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for being so thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s our job. You’ve been a great patient—cooperative and strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been a lot, but I’m glad it’s over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you came through it well. Recovery will take time, but you’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll miss you, but we’re glad you’re going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll miss you all too. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been our privilege. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had this pain for about two days now—diffuse, mostly in the lower belly. I’ve been nauseous and vomiting phlegm. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re not eating by mouth—you’re using your GJ tube for water and meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. I haven’t taken anything by mouth in years. I’ve been trying crushed prochlorperazine and ondansetron, but they’re not helping this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve been using lorazepam and morphine for nausea and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I get really sedated. Still, the pain and nausea don’t go away. This feels like my usual gastroparesis flares, but worse and not responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned no diarrhea, fevers, or urinary symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, bowel movements are regular. No fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. In the ER, your white blood cell count was elevated—14.7—and you had some hematuria on urinalysis. But no signs of infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? The high white count?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we’re watching. But you don’t have fever or chills, and your blood cultures came back negative. So it may just be from inflammation or stress on the body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the CT scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT of your abdomen and pelvis showed no bowel obstruction or acute issue. No sign of another volvulus or blockage. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably just a bad gastroparesis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what it looks like. We’ll manage your symptoms and make sure nothing else develops. We’ve started IV morphine and acetaminophen for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But morphine makes my stomach slower. Could that be making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent point. That’s exactly why we’re planning to taper the morphine and switch to tramadol, which is gentler on gastric motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The pain is still there, but not as intense. Nausea is still bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reduced the IV morphine and started oral tramadol. We’re also continuing lorazepam for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to restart tube feeds? I’m worried about making nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted low-dose tube feeds this morning. So far, you’re tolerating them well. We’ll gradually increase as your symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my white count—is it still high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 14.7 on admission, but it’s coming down. Today it’s 11.2. No infection found, so we think it’s resolving on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray to check for pneumonia, since your white count was up. It was clear—no infection in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for checking. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re looking more comfortable today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Pain is mild now, and I haven’t vomited since yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your white count is now 9.8—back to normal. We’re keeping you on tramadol and acetaminophen as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on lorazepam as needed. We’ve also added prochlorperazine for discharge, in case you need extra help at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’d like to avoid morphine if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep it as a backup, but tramadol is safer for your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we had planned to replace your GJ tube this week. Since you’re here, interventional radiology can do it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot about that. Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube is due for replacement. It’s a quick procedure with sedation. They’ll use imaging to guide it and make sure it’s placed correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your GJ tube was successfully replaced this morning. The new one is in place and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smoothly. You got a little fentanyl for sedation, and the radiologist confirmed placement with contrast. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you. Your pain is well-controlled, nausea has improved, and labs are normal. You’re tolerating full tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medications am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your regular meds: citalopram, levothyroxine, omeprazole. For nausea, lorazepam and now prochlorperazine. For pain, tramadol every four hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you a small supply—10 tablets—for severe pain only. But try to avoid it, as it can slow your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please see your primary care provider this week to review everything and renew your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—was the leukocytosis ever explained?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No clear infection was found. We believe the elevated white count was due to inflammation from your gastroparesis flare. It resolved without antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Thank you for explaining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nutrition team has confirmed your tube feeds are running smoothly. You’re getting full strength and tolerating it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll keep that going at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Your vitals are stable—temperature 98.2, blood pressure 158/100, heart rate 88, oxygen 99% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: BP a bit high, but I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. Keep monitoring it at home. Otherwise, you’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea or pain returns and doesn’t respond to meds, or if you develop fever, vomiting, or tube issues, please call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’ll go home with home health services to help with GJ tube care for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you out shortly. Take care and get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I haven’t taken anything today because I was so nauseated. I only sipped a little water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We gave you some fluids, morphine, and lorazepam in the ER. Your blood pressure is a bit high, but otherwise vitals are stable. We’ll keep you NPO for now and use your GJ tube for feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. My tube’s been working well. But I’m worried—my white count was high last time. Is it bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is elevated—15.9—like before. But you don’t have a fever, and your CT scan showed no infection or blockage. It may be a chronic thing, not an acute infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So it’s not an infection this time either?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The CT showed no bowel obstruction or acute issue. Your pain is most consistent with a gastroparesis flare. We’ll focus on symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Can I get more pain meds soon? The last one’s wearing off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can give another dose of morphine. We’ll monitor how you respond. We also restarted your tube feeds slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The nausea’s still there, but the pain’s less sharp. I haven’t vomited, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
