conversation_lines.text: It’s better—maybe a 4 now. But I’m still nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the anti-nausea meds going. Your labs show low potassium, so we’re replacing that too. It’s common with vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I didn’t know that could happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we want to avoid complications. No imaging today since your symptoms match your usual flares and there’s no sign of blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve had so many scans lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs improved overnight. Potassium is better, and your acidosis is resolving. We’ll keep you on IV meds a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little less nauseous. Can I try sipping water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start small. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance your diet slowly. We’re also switching back to your home omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years since my fundoplication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. And we’re continuing your metoclopramide. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but manageable. I’m on my regular morphine at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll transition you back to that soon. But we need to talk about your pain meds—some, like tramadol and Dilaudid, can worsen gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. I only take Dilaudid when it’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend minimizing those. Work with your oncologist to adjust your morphine if needed. It’s a balance, but important for your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll bring it up at my next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down clear liquids and soft foods. We’re switching all your meds to oral form.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m feeling more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last labs look stable. Hemoglobin is low but unchanged, and liver enzymes are normal. Your cancer-related pain is under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gabapentin and morphine help. My back pain from the bone mets is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your oncologist is aware you’re here. Taxol is on hold for now due to your frequent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired of being in and out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focusing on stabilizing your symptoms. You mentioned Tigan—why did you stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I only tried it once. It didn’t help, so I didn’t keep using it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We won’t restart it. We’ll stick with what works—metoclopramide and prochlorperazine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Ativan helps with the nausea and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep that available. Your heart condition is stable too—still on aspirin and Plavix after your PFO closure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t missed a dose. That TIA scare was scary, but I’ve been okay since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. No new neurological symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing since that one time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. You’ve been on regular food, no vomiting, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea returns or you can’t keep food down, come back. Also, avoid those pain meds we discussed. They can trigger flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to my regular morphine and avoid the others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep your appointments—especially with your oncologist and for your Botox injections for gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have one scheduled next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your exam is soft, no tenderness, and bowel sounds are present.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll leave it for now. If things get bad, I’ll call my GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll send instructions to your home. Focus on small, frequent meals and staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll try to cut back on the strong painkillers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. You’re doing well. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will come by with your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your recent imaging showed improvement in bowel inflammation. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. I was worried it might be something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of obstruction or diverticulitis. This was a gastroparesis flare, and we’ve managed it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s under control for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. Call your team if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to rest and take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll follow up with your primary team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. You came in with severe nausea and abdominal pain, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's right. It's been really bad — I'm vomiting more than five times a day, mostly mucus. I haven’t been able to keep anything down for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your vitals are stable, and your labs show mild acidosis and low bicarbonate, but nothing suggests an infection or organ failure. We think this is another flare of your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? But I just got out of the hospital a week ago. Why is this happening so often now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. One possibility is that your long-acting morphine for bone pain might be slowing your gut even more. We’re going to try reducing how often you take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need that for the pain. The cancer in my bones — it’s intense without it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’ll monitor your pain closely. If the nausea improves, we can adjust safely. For now, we’re giving IV fluids, anti-nausea meds like Reglan and Ativan, and stopping oral intake temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. But I’m so tired of being sick. I’ve lost so much weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted your malnutrition. The gastroenterology team is involved. You mentioned wanting a GJ tube again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had one before. It helped me get nutrition when I couldn’t eat. I want it replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted the team. Since your nausea is improving, you’ve decided to wait and have the tube placed as an outpatient?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if it’s okay. I just don’t want to be stuck here longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ve scheduled the appointment. You’ll need to stop Plavix five days before the procedure, but you’ll restart it when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray yesterday showed no pneumonia or acute issues. But we did see some atelectasis — that’s when part of the lung is slightly collapsed. It’s common if you’re not moving much or breathing deeply due to pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve been having some shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not serious right now. We’ll encourage you to sit up, walk when you can, and do breathing exercises. It should resolve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also wanted to talk about your UTI. Your primary doctor started you on Macrobid, but your urine culture showed it’s resistant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s not working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, so we’ve switched to IV ceftriaxone. You’ll finish a five-day course while you’re here. That should clear it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low, likely from vomiting. We’ve been giving IV potassium, and it’s now stable. You’ll continue oral supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling weaker. Is that why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, low potassium can cause that. We’re correcting it, so you should feel stronger soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have some news. Your stool test came back positive for C. difficile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What is that? Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bacterial infection that causes diarrhea, often after antibiotics. You’ll start oral vancomycin for ten days to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had diarrhea the past few days. That makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll monitor you, but it’s treatable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned rib pain, so we did an X-ray. No fracture, but there’s a small area of atelectasis or possibly early pneumonia at the lung base. You’re not running a fever, so we’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. We’ll keep an eye on your breathing and oxygen levels. Staying mobile helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has improved, and you’re tolerating liquids. That’s great progress. We’re transitioning you back to oral anti-nausea meds like ondansetron and metoclopramide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. I was scared I’d never eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also restarting your regular meds, including morphine for bone pain, but we’ll keep an eye on how it affects your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my oncologist said I could restart Taxol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once your nutrition improves and you’re stable. You’ll follow up with them soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ECG shows your QT interval was prolonged before, so we avoided certain medications. Today it’s 413 ms — much better and safe for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a heart rhythm measure. A long QT can be risky, but yours is now in a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’re eating well, your nausea is controlled, and your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications, especially the vancomycin for C. diff. Take it exactly as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Plavix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume it today. But remember — stop it five days before your GJ tube procedure, then restart after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your oncologist to discuss resuming Taxol. And keep your GI appointment for the feeding tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re alert, your abdomen is soft, and you’ve been walking independently. We’re discharging you home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. It’s been a long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your medications. You’ll have ondansetron for nausea, continue vancomycin for ten days, and all your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll see my doctors soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oncology and GI. Call us if nausea returns, or if you develop fever, severe pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — should I be worried about the C. diff coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As long as you finish the full course and practice good hand hygiene, the risk is low. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep drinking fluids and eating small, frequent meals to help your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It’s hard with the gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why the feeding tube follow-up is so important. It can help with long-term nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m committed to it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll make sure everything is coordinated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re all proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You’re here because of nausea and vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just like last time. I felt okay the day after I got home, but then it came back—nausea, then vomiting. I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. No fever, pain, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just nausea and vomiting. The pain only comes with the vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of gastroparesis and recent discharge, we’ll start with IV fluids and anti-nausea meds. We also need to check if your C. diff treatment is complete.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took the last vancomycin dose yesterday. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that matches your record. We’ll keep monitoring for symptoms. Your labs show low albumin and mild anemia, so malnutrition is a concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been losing weight. I just can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re considering a GJ tube again. It helped before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it did. I was able to get nutrition and felt better. But I was hoping to avoid another procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But given how quickly you relapsed, it might be the best option now to prevent future admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, if it’s the right thing. When would it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it for tomorrow. The interventional radiology team will place it using imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re set to do the GJ tube placement this morning. Any questions before we proceed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep? Is it painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation—fentanyl and midazolam—so you’ll be drowsy and comfortable. Local numbing at the site too. Most patients tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GJ tube was placed successfully. The tip is in the jejunum, and the balloon is inflated in the stomach. We’ll wait 24 hours before using the gastric port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can we start the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start continuous tube feeds tonight through the jejunal port. Nutrition recommends Jevity 1.5 at 50 mL/hour to start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s Jevity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a high-calorie, high-protein formula designed for tube feeding. It has vitamins and minerals too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. WBC is low but not concerning. Potassium and magnesium are normal. We’re watching for refeeding syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s refeeding syndrome?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When someone who’s malnourished starts eating again, the body shifts fluids and electrolytes. We monitor closely and give thiamine to prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So that’s why I’m getting thiamine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Just a precaution. You’re doing well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating the tube feeds well. We’re increasing to 75 mL/hour for 16 hours, then a break.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We want to make sure you’re stable on the feeds and your nausea is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my cancer? I haven’t had treatment in a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not on active chemo now. Your CEA tumor marker was normal, which is reassuring. But we’ll need to follow up with oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on anastrozole and paclitaxel before. Should I restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a conversation for your oncologist. Right now, the priority is stabilizing your nutrition and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your port was accessed today for labs. All levels are stable. No signs of infection or electrolyte issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your imaging. The GJ tube is in the right place. You’re doing well—no vomiting, and you’re tolerating feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try a little food by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can try small amounts of low-fat foods. But the tube will remain your main source of nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making great progress. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the tube feeds at 75 mL/hour for 16 hours. Use Ensure Original three times a day. Add extra water every 6 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—metoclopramide, omeprazole, morphine for pain, and ondansetron if nauseous. But hold off on Denosumab until you see oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why stop Denosumab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s used to protect bones in metastatic cancer, but your team wants to reassess your treatment plan first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. A nurse will visit to help with the tube, and you’ll follow up with gastroenterology and oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Call if you have fever, redness at the tube site, or can’t keep feeds down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my mood has been low. Should I talk to someone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please mention that at your follow-up. Depression and anxiety are common, and we can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure it’s on your follow-up list. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The transport team will take you home shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check in with you next week by phone to make sure things are going smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand your G-tube clogged and you've been feeling really sick since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it clogged yesterday. I tried flushing it, but it ripped and stomach contents spilled out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That must have been distressing. You started having nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain after that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nonstop. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve vomited. And now there’s this burning rash where the fluid touched my skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like irritation from the tube contents. We’ll clean it and start treatment. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. Just the pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your vitals are stable. We’ve checked your labs and found your potassium is a bit low, so we’re giving you some IV fluids and potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be able to eat or feed through the tube soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. The tube is damaged, so we’ll need to replace it. The interventional radiology team will do that tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? This is the second time in months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s frustrating. We’ll use a larger tube this time to reduce the chance of clogging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The team replaced your GJ tube this morning with a 16 French one. It’s now in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to start feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slowly tomorrow. Your stomach needs time to adjust after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the rash? It still burns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started a cream called betamethasone and an antibiotic ointment to prevent infection. It should improve in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your tube feeds today with a new formula called Osmolite 1.5. It’s easier on your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will this one cause less nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. We’ll go slow and monitor you closely. If you tolerate it, we’ll increase the rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back positive for C. difficile. That could be contributing to your nausea and loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a recurrence. We’re starting oral vancomycin for 10 days to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me feel better faster?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should reduce the diarrhea and help your gut heal. We’ll keep monitoring your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well with the feeds. The vancomycin seems to be helping—your stools are less frequent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The rash is also less red. But I felt a gurgle in my tube this morning and then it stopped draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check it. Sometimes they can clog again, especially with formula changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry, but the tube is clogged again. We’ll need to replace it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? This is so discouraging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll use an 18 French tube this time—larger to prevent clogging. The team will do it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the new 18 French tube was placed successfully. It’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we restart feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart Osmolite 1.5 at a low rate and increase as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating the feeds well. Your nausea has improved, and your labs are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How long before I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If this continues, likely in two days. We’ll finish your vancomycin course and make sure the tube stays open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to keep using this new formula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we think Osmolite 1.5 is better for your gastroparesis. We’ll send it home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your rash is improving. We’ll keep using the creams for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The betamethasone says not to use it long-term. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’ll stop it after two weeks—it can thin the skin. The Bactroban will continue for infection prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish a 10-day course. We’re prescribing four more days to complete it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. The tube is working, feeds are at goal, and your pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all goes well. We’ll finalize your discharge plan today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have help at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home health will assist with wound care and tube management. They’ll teach your husband too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Gastroenterology and oncology will see you soon. We’ll send records and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. Thank you for fixing the tube and helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: use the creams as directed, finish the vancomycin, and keep using Osmolite 1.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And flush the tube regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Flush with water before and after feeds and meds. Call if it clogs or the rash worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re also continuing your regular meds: omeprazole, metoclopramide, gabapentin, and pain meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Denosumab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume your usual schedule. Oncology will manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge nurse will go over wound care and give you supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send instructions on how to clean the skin around the tube and change the dressing daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I moisten the dressing before removing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to avoid trauma. Use saline to dampen it first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep monitoring for signs of infection: increased redness, swelling, or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’re confident you’ll do well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Take it easy, follow the plan, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your husband can call the on-call team if he has questions about tube care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: He’ll be glad to know that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well, and take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had terrible right back pain—up to a 10—and my right leg felt weak. Also, there’s this painful rash on my right side with big blisters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The rash—has it changed over time? Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. The blisters have been there for about three weeks. I’ve never had shingles, and this is the first time I’ve had a rash like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check it out. Given your history of metastatic breast cancer, we need to rule out infection or nerve involvement. We’ve started you on vancomycin and Zosyn just in case it’s a bacterial infection like bullous impetigo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it shingles? I’m worried it might be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. The rash is on one side and blistering, which fits. But we’re treating it cautiously until we get more info. We unroofed one blister for culture, but results will take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the back pain? It’s been sharp and constant. My leg felt weak when the pain was worst.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRI of your spine. It was a bit blurry because of movement, but we didn’t see any spinal cord compression. There is extensive bone metastasis, though, and some new lesions in your spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So the pain is from the cancer spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The metastases are contributing, and there’s also nerve root thickening. But no urgent compression, which is good. We’ve given you Dilaudid for pain and will keep adjusting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My leg feels stronger now, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We also checked your chest and belly with X-rays. Your PICC line is in place, and your feeding tube is where it should be. No pneumonia or bowel issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My J-tube has been acting up. I’ve had trouble with it clogging before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed. The team is monitoring it. We may need to replace it if it’s not working. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and nutrition support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, maybe a 7 now. The meds help, but it’s not gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep working on it. Your labs are stable—no infection signs in blood. But your phosphate was low, so we’re replacing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the rash getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not spreading. We’re treating it as shingles with possible bacterial infection. We’ll continue antibiotics until we’re sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my feeding tube? I rely on that for nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to replace it tomorrow. The current one is clogged. We’ll put in a wider one to prevent future blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get light sedation. It’s a quick procedure. The new tube will have a larger lumen so it’s less likely to clog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the CT results. Your liver metastases have actually improved—fewer and smaller lesions. That’s a good sign your chemotherapy is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. But there are new bone spots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two new sclerotic lesions in the right pelvis. They could be new metastases. We’ll discuss with oncology, but no immediate intervention is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the rash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still consistent with shingles. We’re keeping you on antibiotics just in case there’s a bacterial infection on top of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a bit weak. Is it from not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. You’ve been on IV fluids, but we know you’ve had malnutrition. That’s why replacing the feeding tube is so important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your feeding tube was successfully replaced this morning. It’s an 18 French tube, larger to prevent clogging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How soon can I start feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow today—low rate, see how you tolerate it. We’ll use Osmolite 1.5, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? Are we still sure it’s shingles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still presuming shingles with possible bacterial complication. We’ll continue the antibiotics for now and reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is better—maybe a 5 now. Can I switch back to my home pain meds soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re already transitioning you back to Dilaudid and morphine. We’ll make sure you’re comfortable before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The feeding tube is working, and you’re tolerating nutrition. The rash is starting to scab over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, tomorrow. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled, you’re on the right meds, and home care is set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I continue chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oncologist wants you to resume paclitaxel on the 3-on, 1-off schedule. We’ll coordinate that through outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop the IV ones today. You’ll finish a course of oral vancomycin at home for the rash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about managing everything at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a nurse to help with the tube and meds. And your DNR status is documented—we’ll respect your wishes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’ll discharge you this morning. Keep taking the vancomycin, use the pain meds as needed, and follow up with oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.
